content: In December 2021, a technical meeting was convened to explore the role of infection, inflammation, and genetic ancestry as potential factors influencing adjustments in hemoglobin concentrations for defining anemia, particularly at the population level. This meeting also addressed considerations related to blood sampling and analytical methods used for hemoglobin determination. Participants were required to declare any relevant interests prior to their participation, and conflicts of interest were publicly disclosed at the start of each meeting. No significant conflicts were recorded. A series of virtual meetings of the second Guideline Development Group (GDG) took place in June and July 2022. The objectives included formulating normative statements on the use and interpretation of hemoglobin concentrations for assessing anemia in individuals and populations, considering factors such as benefits, harms, values, preferences, feasibility, equity, ethics, acceptability, and resource requirements. The group also aimed to identify research gaps and discuss implementation and evaluation considerations for the guideline. Evidence informing hemoglobin cutoffs was derived from analyses of healthy population databases, general population databases, and systematic reviews. Efforts were made to identify unpublished or ongoing studies by contacting international organizations and systematically searching databases such as the National Library of Medicine and the WHO International Clinical Trials Registry Platform. No language restrictions were applied during the search. Evidence summaries and profiles were prepared using the GRADE approach to assess the overall certainty of the evidence. GRADE evaluates study design, limitations, consistency of results, directness of evidence, and precision of effect estimates. However, the GRADE approach could only be applied to a subset of the questions. The GDG interpreted the evidence using the DECIDE framework, which incorporates intervention effects, values, resources, equity, acceptability, and feasibility criteria to guide the formulation of normative statements. The certainty of direct evidence for critical outcomes was moderate, but for three questions, it was considered very low. During the second GDG meetings, discussions focused on hemoglobin cutoffs for infants and children aged 6–59 months. A proposal for a single cutoff of <105 g/L for the entire age group was presented and voted on, differing from the WHO's initial proposal of separate cutoffs for 6–23 months and 24–59 months. Concerns were raised about the single cutoff due to mixed evidence and unclear health criteria. Subsequent analysis confirmed consistent differences in hemoglobin concentrations between the two age groups, supporting the need for separate cutoffs. The WHO proposed a gradual increase in cutoffs from 105 g/L at 23 months to 110 g/L at 59 months and 115 g/L at 5 years of age. A third GDG meeting in June 2023 discussed the rationale for separating hemoglobin cutoffs into two groups (6–23 months and 24–59 months). The rationale included maintaining consistency with health criteria for other age groups, evidence of consistent differences in hemoglobin concentrations between the two groups, differences in growth and nutrient requirements, and additional analysis supporting the separation. The proposal was approved with eight votes in favor, one against, and two abstentions. The WHO Secretariat managed competing interests according to established guidelines. All participants submitted declarations of interest and verbally disclosed any potential conflicts at the start of each meeting. The names of GDG members and meeting objectives were published on the WHO website for public notice and comment. No additional information on potential biases was identified from the public notice. The WHO Secretariat will continue to monitor research developments in anemia detection, diagnosis, and control, particularly in areas with limited or low-quality evidence. If an update to the guideline is warranted, the Department of Nutrition and Food Safety will coordinate the process following formal WHO procedures.
